channel.title: Jay McDaniel — The Valuation Letter
channel.description: Answer-first writing on valuation, business divorce, and exit for closely held companies.

item.title: How Key-Man Discounts Actually Work When Fixing the Value of a Business
item.description: When one person is the business, a key-man discount is real — but it is never automatic, and the other side will fight its size. It sticks only when the record shows that the enterprise's earnings genuinely depend on a single owner and that the dependence cannot be cured at reasonable cost.

item.title: The Owners Never Signed Post-Employment Restrictions. What That Does to Value.
item.description: A departing owner who can compete tomorrow is a discount the buyer will demand today. When the owners never signed non-competition or non-solicitation covenants, the missing protection shows up directly in the number — because a buyer cannot pay full price for goodwill that can walk out the door and set up across the street.

item.title: Valuing a Business in a Matrimonial Case: Why the Number Differs From a Buyout
item.description: Same company, different standard of value, different result. A matrimonial valuation and a shareholder buyout can produce very different numbers for the identical business, because they answer different legal questions — and the matrimonial lawyer who misses the distinction leaves value on the table or overpays for it.

item.title: Fair Value vs. Fair Market Value: The Discount Fight That Decides the Case
item.description: Marketability and minority discounts are where many closely held disputes are actually won or lost. Which standard governs is the first fight. Fair market value generally allows those discounts; fair value, the standard in most oppression and dissenters'-rights cases, usually does not — and that single choice will swing the number by a third or more.

item.title: When the IRS Challenges Your Gift-Tax Valuation: Building a Record That Holds
item.description: The appraisal that survives examination is built before the gift, not after the notice. A defensible gift-tax valuation is a contemporaneous, qualified appraisal that documents its assumptions, discounts, and methodology at the transfer date — so that when the IRS challenges the number, the record answers the challenge instead of inviting it.

item.title: Exit Readiness: The Three Value Gaps Owners Discover Too Late
item.description: Owner dependence, customer concentration, and undocumented process quietly cap the multiple a buyer will pay — and owners usually discover them only in diligence, when it is too late to fix. Closed years before a sale rather than months, each of the three converts personal value into transferable enterprise value the market will actually pay for.

item.title: Deadlock Isn't a Dead End: Using the Buy-Sell to Force Price Discovery
item.description: A well-built shotgun clause turns stalemate into a number. When owners deadlock, a buy-sell that forces one side to name a price at which it will either buy or sell breaks the impasse by making price discovery unavoidable — while a badly built one hands the leverage to whoever moves first or has the deeper pockets.
